name: Hawai'i Creole English
sweep_summary: Hawai'i Creole English is not in the catalog and the sweep's single title-hit is a false positive: Glottolog ref 447982 (Brenier & Michaelis 2005, 'Syntax-prosody mismatch and copula doubling') was machine-tagged hwc from the keyword 'copula' (Glottolog's record says so); the open author PDF was fetched sources and read - it is about the American English 'ISIS' construction in the Switchboard corpus, never mentions Hawai'i, creole or pidgin, and the prosody involved is phrasal prominence on the copula, not word stress. Recommend removing the hwc tag from this reference locally. Beyond the target list, the open-access Drager 2012 overview (fetched sources, read) presupposes a stressed/unstressed contrast in Pidgin (vowel quality and non-reduction depend on stress) but states no placement rule, and points to Sakoda & Siegel 2004 'Hawai'i Creole: phonology' pp. 222-223 (Mouton, paywalled, not read) as the primary description - that chapter is the high-priority acquisition for a first-hand stress statement. APiCS survey/structure pages for Hawai'i Creole (checked) contain no stress or prosody feature. No first-hand word-stress placement statement was read in this sweep. Files with.gr, APiCS, Wikipedia) were used.

sources.citation: Drager, Katie. 2012. Pidgin and Hawai'i English: An overview. International Journal of Language, Translation and Intercultural Communication 1: 61-73.
sources.quote: In Pidgin, however, there are no non-prevocalic [r]-colored vowels except for /ɝ/ as in nurse, which in the basilect is found in monosyllabic words or stressed positions (Sakoda & Siegel 2004: 222-223). The vowel in words like north and force are realized without [r] coloring, and the vowel quality depends on stress; it is realized as [ɔ] in monosyllabic words and stressed syllables and as [o] in unstressed syllables. Likewise, unstressed vowels are not realized as [ə] as in comma or [ɨ] as in horses but as a full vowel [ɑ] or [e], respectively.
sources.note: Presupposes a stressed/unstressed syllable distinction in Pidgin (it conditions vowel quality and the absence of reduction to schwa) but gives no statement of where word stress falls. Points to Sakoda & Siegel 2004: 222-223 as the primary phonological description.
